items.title: 19.1.3 The Concept of Genes and Alleles

source_refs.note: Topic 19.1.3 (PDF 118-119); Figure 19.5 is replaced by the original diagram.

blocks.text: In 1909 the Danish botanist Wilhelm Johannsen introduced the term 'gene' for the basic unit of heredity. A gene was later found to be 'a short segment of DNA which encodes the sequence of amino acids of a particular polypeptide'. Not all the DNA in a chromosome carries messages for sequencing amino acids; short segments of it, the genes, encode proteins. The location of a gene on a chromosome is its locus (plural loci).

blocks.alt: A pair of homologous chromosomes, one blue from one parent and one red from the other, with matching yellow bands at three loci: A on one and a on the other, b and B at a second locus, and D on both at a third.
blocks.caption: Alleles at matching loci on a homologous pair (original diagram after Figure 19.5).
blocks.long_description: Only short segments of the DNA in a chromosome, the genes, code for proteins, and each gene has a fixed location, its locus. Homologous chromosomes carry the same genes in the same order, so the alleles of a gene, its alternative forms, lie at the same locus on both: if one chromosome has an allele for eye colour at a locus, its homologue has an allele for eye colour at the same locus. The two alleles may differ, as A and a, or be the same, as D and D.

blocks.text: On homologous chromosomes the alternative forms of a gene, its alleles, lie at the same locus. If one chromosome has an allele for eye colour at a particular locus, its homologue carries an allele for the same character at the same locus.

blocks.prompt: What is a locus, and where are the two alleles of a gene found?
blocks.explanation: A locus is the fixed position of a gene on a chromosome. The two alleles are at the same locus on the two homologous chromosomes.

items: Gene: DNA segment coding for one polypeptide; locus: its position.
Alleles of a gene sit at the same locus on homologues.
